newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka rebels strike at army after setback.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka rebels strike at army after setback.

text.p: Separatist Tamil Tiger guerrillas, driven by soldiers from their Kilinochchi stronghold in northern Sri Lanka, have hit back elsewhere with deadly mine attacks on troops, the military and rebels said on Tuesday.

The guerrillas' Voice of Tigers radio said a rebel landmine exploded under an army vehicle in Jaffna town on Monday morning, killing seven soldiers. Jaffna is the rebels' former northern stronghold now under army control.
Later the same day, another rebel landmine attack on a police convoy at Meesalai near Jaffna town killed four policemen and wounded 27, a military spokesman said.
"The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) have stepped up attacks on government soldiers in other areas (outside of Kilinochchi)," rebel radio said.
A military spokesman said on Tuesday that troops were mopping up scattered rebel resistance as they consolidated their positions in Kilinochchi, which was empty of civilians.
"We're moving very carefully, clearing and consolidating," the spokesman told Reuters.

The LTTE's official newspapers Eelanatham and Eelanadu, published in the northern rebel territory of the Wanni, admitted for the first time in their Tuesday issues that Kilinochchi had fallen to government troops.
"Government troops have entered town," Eelanatham said. "But Tigers are engaged in fighting troops in areas near the town."
The town's population of about 200,000 minority Tamils had fled to safer areas, mostly to the south, where Western aid agencies operated temporary shelters, aid worker said.
Some of them were refugees from Jaffna who had fled to Kilinochchi when the army began its offensive to take Jaffna late last year, they said.
Chief military spokesman Brigadier Sarath Munasinghe told Reuters there was no immediate plan to invite the refugees to return to Kilinochchi.
"The operation is purely military at this stage. We do not have a time frame yet for moving civilians back to Kilinochchi," Munasinghe said.
Soldiers backed by tanks, artillery and air support seized Kilinochchi, 285 km (180 miles) north of the capital Colombo, on Sunday after a week of fierce fighting.
The army lost 269 soldiers in the offensive while more than 700 rebels were killed and over 800 wounded, the military spokesman said. About 300 soldiers were wounded.
The LTTE gave no death toll, but it said on Sunday that 90 of its fighters had died. With reporters banned from the war zone, no independent verification is possible.

Former rebel Douglas Devananda, who now heads the moderate Eelam Peoples' Democratic Party in parliament, said he believed the LTTE would move its main base to the coastal town of Mullaitivu, 40 km (25 miles) southeast of Kilinochchi.
In July, the LTTE overran a strategic army camp at Mullaitivu, killing or capturing almost its entire garrison of well over 1,000 men to end the military's presence in the area.
"They cleared Mullaitivu (of the army) expecting to fall back there in case of an army attack on Kilinochchi," Devananda said.
"I think the LTTE leadership will now operate from Mullaitivu. It's safer for them. On one side there is the sea, on the other there are civilians," Devananda said.
The LTTE, fighting a 13-year-old war for an independent Tamil homeland in the island's north and east, has said a large number of Tamils moved to Mullaitivu after the guerrillas took the camp.
